title: The NTT spinning like a top
caption: The New Technology Telescope turning during a 30-second exposure, La Silla Observatory
celestial: Landscape photograph; the source does not name the site

recognition.text: ESO Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: The angular enclosure of the New Technology Telescope (NTT) at ESO's La Silla Observatory in Chile is smeared by motion, because the telescope was turning toward its target during a 30-second exposure. Its outside is made of sharp angles rather than the rounded dome most observatories use.

That shape was groundbreaking when the NTT opened in 1989, and its features have since been widely copied, including by ESO's Very Large Telescope. The design aims for the best possible image quality. Carefully controlled ventilation moves air across the telescope and reduces the blurring caused by turbulence inside the building. The large flaps that are part of this system can just be made out in the blur.

The mirror, 3.58 meters across, was never thought of as especially big, but its design was highly innovative. It is flexible and is adjusted continuously to keep a perfect shape, so it cannot sag or flex enough to harm the image. ESO and the NTT pioneered this approach, called active optics, and it is now standard on modern telescopes.

understand.summary: A ground-based photograph by Malte Tewes, taken in visible light with a 30-second exposure. The colors are those the camera recorded.
understand.eye: The eye would see the building turn smoothly, while the camera's 30-second exposure records the whole movement at once as a blur.

explore: The NTT carries two instruments. SOFI, short for Son of ISAAC after a VLT instrument, is a spectrograph and imaging camera that works in infrared light, and EFOSC2 is a spectrograph and camera built to detect faint objects. La Silla sits 2400 meters up in the southern Atacama Desert, some 600 kilometers to the north of Santiago de Chile. The photograph is by Malte Tewes, an astronomer at Lausanne's Ecole Polytechnique Fédérale in Switzerland, and he shared it through the Your ESO Pictures Flickr group.
alt: An angular telescope building blurred by its own rotation, with large flaps just visible in the blur.
